**1. Which criminal provision(s) are likely to be invoked?** | Issue | Likely statutory provision(s) | Typical section(s) of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) | |-------|------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------| | **Cheating** | **Section 420 IPC** – “Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property.” This is the core offence when a person dishonestly induces another to deliver money or property. | **Sec. 420** | | **Cheating with a false document / mis‑representation of a written instrument** | **Section 467 IPC** – “Forgery of valuable security, will, etc.” If the partner alleges that a false document (e.g., a fake invoice, agreement, or bank‑statement) was used to obtain money, Sec. 467 may be added. | **Sec. 467** | | **Cheating by inducing delivery of property through a false statement** | **Section 406 IPC** – “Criminal breach of trust” (if the partner claims the brother mis‑used property that was entrusted to him). | **Sec. 406** | | **Criminal breach of trust** | **Section 409 IPC** – “Criminal breach of trust by a public servant, banker, merchant or agent.” If the brother acted in a fiduciary capacity (e.g., as a partner in a firm). | **Sec. 409** | | **Other ancillary provisions** | **Section 120B IPC** – “Punishment for criminal conspiracy” (if the partner alleges that the brother conspired with a third party). | **Sec. 120B** | > **Bottom line:** The police will most commonly register the FIR under **Section 420 IPC** (cheating). Depending on the facts they may also add sections 467, 406/ 409, 120B etc. --- **2. What happens after the FIR is lodged?** 1. **First Information Report (FIR)** – The police record the complaint and assign a case number. 2. **Investigation** – The police may summon your brother for questioning, seize documents, and prepare a **charge‑sheet** (or file a **final report** if they find no case). 3. **Arrest** – Under **Section 41 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC)**, a police officer may arrest a person without a warrant if: * The offence is cognizable (which cheating under Sec. 420 is), **and** * The officer has reasonable grounds to believe that the person has committed the offence. If your brother is arrested, he will be produced before the **magistrate** within **24 hours** (excluding the time taken for the journey) as per **Section 57 CrPC**. --- **3. How to obtain bail?** Bail in India is governed by **Chapter XV of the CrPC** (Sections 436‑450). The procedure differs slightly depending on whether the offence is **bailable** or **non‑bailable**. | Nature of offence | Bail provision | Typical bail conditions | |-------------------|----------------|--------------------------| | **Bailable offence** (e.g., Sec. 420 is *non‑bailable* but some lesser cheating offences may be bailable) | **Section 436 CrPC** – Right to bail on personal bond or surety. | The police or court may release the accused on a personal bond (with or without surety) if the offence is bailable. | | **Non‑bailable offence** (most cheating cases, including Sec. 420) | **Section 437 CrPC** – Bail may be granted by the **court of session** (or the magistrate) after considering factors such as:
• Nature & gravity of the offence
• Likelihood of the accused fleeing
• Possibility of tampering with evidence
• Antecedent criminal record | The court may release the accused on **personal bond** (usually with a surety of ₹10,000–₹50,000, depending on the court) and may impose conditions such as:
• Surrender of passport
• Reporting to police station weekly
• No contact with the complainant or witnesses | **Practical steps to secure bail:** 1. **Engage a criminal defence lawyer immediately.** *A competent lawyer can file a bail application on the same day of arrest (or as soon as the accused is produced before the magistrate).* 2. **Prepare the bail‑application documents:** * **Affidavit** of the accused stating his address, occupation, and that he will cooperate with the investigation. * **Surety bond** (cash or surety‑person) as required by the court. * **Undertaking** to appear before the court whenever summoned and not to tamper with evidence or influence witnesses. 3. **File the bail petition:** * If the arrest is made by the **police**, the first hearing is before the **Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM)** or **Judicial Magistrate of First Class** (depending on the jurisdiction). The lawyer will file an application under **Section 437 CrPC**. * If the **charge‑sheet** has already been filed (i.e., the case is in the **court of session**), bail is applied for under **Section 439 CrPC** (bail after charge‑sheet). 4. **Possible grounds the court will consider for granting bail:** * The offence, though non‑bailable, is **non‑violent** and the accused is not a flight risk. * The accused has **stable family ties**, a **permanent address**, and **no prior criminal record**. * The investigation is **document‑based** (e.g., bank statements, contracts) and the risk of evidence tampering is low. * The complainant’s claim is **disputed** and the accused is willing to **co‑operate**. 5. **If bail is denied:** * The lawyer can **appeal** to the **High Court** under **Section 439(2) CrPC** within **30 days** of the order. * The High Court may grant bail if it is satisfied that the reasons for denial are not justified. --- **4.
